(2026) quantified this through the Goal Attention Ratio (GAR), showing 27-48% drops over 50 turns, while their residual stream probes reveal that goal information persists (AUC up to 0.98) even as the attention channel closes. This creates a natural hypothesis: if the information is in the residual stream but attention fails to access it, a learnable gate on the residual connection should recover it. We implement this hypothesis as ThreadGate, a per-layer gating module trained with joint NTP and GAR objectives. ThreadGate successfully optimizes GAR during training (0.02 to 0.48), and this improvement transfers perfectly when evaluated on same-distribution text at inference (GAR-ours = 0.49). However, on model-generated text, GAR-ours collapses to 0.016—a 30× gap driven by text distribution shift. Our central finding is that attention patterns learned under teacher-forced contexts (gold text) do not generalize to autoregressive generation contexts (model-generated text), the classic exposure bias phenomenon. This distribution shift is structural, independent of loss design or gating architecture. We further identify two coupled mechanisms that amplify the shift: (1) NTP loss dominates gate gradients, causing gates to learn reverse turn conditioning (suppressing at early turns where GAR is high, becoming passive at late turns where intervention is needed); (2) at inference time, gates attenuate residual updates by only 2-7%, far too weak to shift attention patterns. Four-way ablation (ThreadGate vs. Uniform Gate vs. LoRA-only vs. Base) confirms gating provides zero incremental contribution. Notably, this 30× gap is specific to GAR-ours (last-token attention to goals); GAR-Dongre (all-token attention) shows uniformly low values regardless of text distribution, revealing that exposure bias selectively disrupts summary-position attention patterns. Combined with Dongre et al.'s independent failure of goal re-injection, our results provide the first empirical characterization of how text distribution shift (exposure bias) selectively destroys attention patterns learned through auxiliary losses, and identify the specific mechanisms through which this vulnerability manifests.
